Computer Engineering · 2025

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
Sponsored project context
This is a sponsored engineering project with Partnerships for Global Surgery, developed by a seven-person Harvey Mudd Engineering Clinic team in collaboration with clinical and engineering advisors. The project responds to the cost, fragility, maintenance, training, and supply-chain barriers that can limit access to pediatric rigid bronchoscopy equipment.
The team is designing for pediatric patients from approximately 9 months to 6 years old. Affordability goals place the desired system cost below $5,000, with a required ceiling below $10,000. These are targets, not demonstrated final-device performance.
The proposed system contains five connected subsystems: the rigid bronchoscope tube, handle, distal-camera endoscope, forceps, and suction. Current work has concentrated on the tube, handle, and endoscope; forceps development, manufacturing, and full-system testing remain future work.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
My contributions
I have worked on three endoscope-centered subteams:

Camera and handle architecture: selected a miniature distal camera with teammates and generated handle concepts for controlled camera positioning.
Camera cleaning: prototyped approaches for restoring visibility when saliva or mucus obscures the distal window.
Thermal characterization: helped develop and perform heat testing to understand camera temperature rise and guide cooling and packaging decisions.

Because the project is collaborative and ongoing, these contributions sit within a broader team effort spanning the bronchoscope tube, ergonomics, forceps, suction, manufacturing, and verification.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
From CAD to manufactured hardware








Figure 1: CAD model showing the handle, viewing head, and long rigid shaft.



CAD iteration. The model establishes the overall shaft, viewing head, handle, and internal packaging envelope before committing to manufactured hardware.








Figure 2: Manufactured pediatric bronchoscope prototype.



Current hardware prototype. This developmental device provides a basis for checking reach, packaging, handling, and interfaces. It is not the completed or clinically validated system.


The CAD and hardware prototype represent the design at different levels of fidelity. The CAD model makes geometry and component placement easier to revise; physical prototypes reveal assembly, handling, and interface issues that are difficult to judge from a screen. Both are expected to change as testing continues.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
System architecture
The current bronchoscope concept uses a 30 cm rigid tube with a 5.7 mm outer diameter and 5.0 mm inner diameter for the smallest target patient group. The internal lumen is divided into three channels: a 2.6 mm camera channel and two larger working channels that can carry forceps and suction. The channels end before the distal tip so the operator can see instruments as they enter the airway model.
The overall design must maintain visualization while supporting tool manipulation, ventilation and anesthesia flow, and suction. That makes the project a system-integration problem rather than only a camera-packaging problem.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
Miniature endoscope integration
The endoscope concept places a 2.0 mm distal camera with integrated illumination inside a roughly 2.5 mm outer-diameter rigid encasing. That leaves very little radial space for alignment, wiring, a protective sapphire window, sealing features, and manufacturing tolerance.





flowchart LR
  CLIN[Clinical visualization needs] --> OPT[Camera, window, and illumination]
  OPT --> SHAFT[2.5 mm rigid shaft envelope]
  SHAFT --> HANDLE[Handle and viewing-direction mechanism]
  HANDLE --> USE[Usable field of view]

  CLEAN[Cleaning and sterilization] --> SEAL[Sealing and material choices]
  SEAL --> SHAFT
  HEAT[Camera and LED heat] --> OPT
  DUR[Repeated-use durability] --> HANDLE






The selected camera is designed to provide a 720 × 720 color feed at 30 frames per second through a USB backend. A hardware control supports white-balance calibration. These capabilities still need to be evaluated in representative lighting, working-distance, fogging, and simulated-airway conditions.
A preliminary bench observation recorded a camera temperature of approximately 47.2 °C after 15 minutes of continuous operation. That result informs the design, but it is not a completed thermal verification. The planned test places the camera in a body-temperature mock-airway environment and compares its maximum temperature against the team’s draft acceptance criterion.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
Design questions








Area
Current engineering question
Evidence needed




Camera packaging
Can the camera, wiring, and protective features fit inside the shaft without damaging the optical path?
Cross-sectional fit checks, assembly trials, and tolerance analysis


Visualization
Is the 720 × 720 feed functionally sufficient at clinically relevant distances?
White-balance, frame-rate, latency, working-distance, and simulated-use tests


Distal sealing
Can the camera be protected behind a sealed window without creating glare, distortion, or fluid ingress?
Leak testing and optical comparison before and after sealing


Thermal behavior
Do the camera and LEDs remain within acceptable temperatures during a procedure?
Instrumented temperature testing over the expected operating time


Cleaning
Can visibility be restored quickly after simulated saliva or mucus obscures the distal window?
Timed cleaning cycles and before/after image scoring


Handling
Does the handle support controlled positioning and viewing-direction adjustment?
Ergonomic evaluation and repeatability testing with clinicians


Integrated use
Can users locate and retrieve representative foreign bodies through the live video feed?
Simulated-airway trials with forceps, suction, fog, and representative objects

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
Engineering trade-offs

Optical access versus protection
A protective window can isolate the camera from moisture and cleaning chemicals, but every additional optical interface can introduce reflection, fogging, contamination, or distortion. Window material, thickness, surface finish, and camera spacing therefore affect both sealing and image quality.


Small diameter versus assembly margin
The narrow shaft is valuable for pediatric use, but the difference between the camera diameter and tube diameter leaves little room for alignment and tolerance. A design that fits nominal CAD dimensions may still be difficult to assemble consistently, so prototype fit checks are essential.


Illumination versus heat
More LED output can improve visibility, but it also adds heat inside a confined metal package. Illumination performance must therefore be evaluated together with temperature rise rather than as a separate subsystem.


Reuse versus serviceability
Sealing the device permanently may improve protection, while a serviceable design may be easier to repair or replace. The eventual architecture must balance cleaning, durability, manufacturing, sterilization, and the practical maintenance capabilities of the intended hospitals.

title: Pediatric Bronchoscope
text:
Current stage and verification plan
The project is currently in requirements development, detailed design, and preliminary prototype evaluation. The fall work establishes system architecture, design criteria, early prototypes, and test protocols; it does not represent a finished device.
Planned spring work includes manufacturing the current design, testing it in simulated bronchoscopy conditions, revising failed or weak areas, and producing a later prototype for another round of verification. Draft tests cover usability, thermal behavior, image quality, camera cleaning, and foreign-object removal. Results will determine which requirements are actually met and which subsystems need further iteration.
Even after those tests, additional professional, regulatory, reprocessing, and clinical work would be required before the system could be considered ready for patient use.

title: MuddSub AUV Electronics
text:
The vehicle
MuddSub is Harvey Mudd College’s student-run autonomous underwater robotics team. The team designs and builds Alfie, an AUV intended to perceive its environment, navigate independently, and complete RoboSub competition tasks.
That mission makes the electrical system a tightly coupled part of the vehicle. Power electronics must support propulsion and compute loads; the signal architecture must connect sensors, thrusters, and higher-level autonomy; and every board must fit inside a pressure-conscious, serviceable mechanical package.

title: MuddSub AUV Electronics
text:
Rev. 1 power and signal boards








Figure 1: MuddSub Power Board Revision 1 render.



Power Board Rev. 1. Distributes energy from separate thruster and electronics batteries and generates regulated rails for vehicle compute, navigation, tether, and control hardware.








Figure 2: MuddSub Signal Board Revision 1 render.



Signal Board Rev. 1. Centers the real-time interfaces around a Teensy 4.1, with thruster PWM and breakouts for the serial buses used across the vehicle.


These are team-designed boards. My work as a PCB team member includes helping turn subsystem requirements into reviewable schematics and layouts, checking interfaces between boards, and supporting verification before the electronics are sealed inside the vehicle.

title: MuddSub AUV Electronics
text:
Electrical architecture





flowchart LR
  TB[Thruster battery] --> PWR[Power board]
  EB[Electronics battery] --> PWR
  PWR --> R12[12 V rail]
  PWR --> R5[5 V rail]
  PWR --> R33[3.3 V rail]
  R12 --> JET[Jetson compute]
  R5 --> DVL[DVL + peripherals]
  R33 --> SIG[Signal board]
  SIG --> PWM[8-channel thruster PWM]
  SIG --> BUS[I²C · SPI · UART]
  PWM --> THR[Thrusters]






The power board accepts independent propulsion and electronics battery inputs. Switching regulators create the voltage rails needed by the Jetson computer, Doppler velocity log, tether hardware, and signal electronics. Keeping these loads organized on a common board simplifies distribution while making rail status and inter-board connections easier to inspect.
The signal board provides the low-level connection between the vehicle computer and physical hardware. A Teensy 4.1 produces PWM commands for eight thrusters and exposes I²C, SPI, UART, digital I/O, relay, and hardware-kill connections for vehicle subsystems.

title: MuddSub AUV Electronics
text:
My contributions

PCB design and review
I contribute to translating system-level needs into board requirements, reviewing schematics and layouts, and checking connector pinouts and power assumptions across the electrical stack. The goal is not only a board that routes successfully, but a board the team can assemble, probe, debug, and revise.


Bring-up and verification
My validation work is organized around staged bring-up: inspect assembly and continuity first, apply current-limited power, verify each regulated rail, then add the controller and connected subsystems. Signal-board checks include programmed PWM outputs, serial-bus connectivity, connector mapping, and safe behavior through the hardware-kill path.


Vehicle integration
I also contribute outside the PCB boundary. Chassis layout, waterproofing, buoyancy, connector access, cable routing, and serviceability all affect whether the electronics can operate reliably underwater. Those mechanical constraints feed back into board shape, mounting-hole placement, connector orientation, and test access.

title: Lab 6: SPI and the Internet of Things
text: This lab connects an STM32L432KC microcontroller, a DS1722 temperature sensor, and an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module to create a browser-controlled temperature monitor. The STM32 reads the sensor through a CMSIS-based SPI driver and communicates with the ESP8266 over UART. The webpage provides temperature information and controls for the onboard LED.

title: Lab 6: SPI and the Internet of Things
text: This lab connects an STM32L432KC microcontroller, a DS1722 temperature sensor, and an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module to create a browser-controlled temperature monitor. The STM32 reads the sensor through a CMSIS-based SPI driver and communicates with the ESP8266 over UART. The webpage provides temperature information and controls for the onboard LED.

title: Lab 6: SPI and the Internet of Things
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
SPI1 uses PA5 for SCLK, PB4 for MISO, and PB5 for MOSI. PB0 controls the DS1722’s active-high chip enable. The interface uses eight-bit transfers with CPOL = 0 and CPHA = 1, so SCLK idles low and data is sampled on falling edges.
The sensor is configured for continuous 12-bit measurements. Each temperature request reads the LSB and MSB registers in separate transactions. CE stays high while an address and a dummy byte are transmitted, then returns low after the transfer finishes.

title: Lab 6: SPI and the Internet of Things
text:
Technical Documentation
The portfolio and lab documentation are available in my GitHub repository.

Schematic


Expand to see schematic







Figure 1: DS1722 temperature-sensor connections.




The DS1722’s VDDD, VDDA, and SERMODE pins connect to 3.3 V, and its ground connects to the MCU ground. SERMODE selects SPI operation. CE connects to PB0, SCLK to PA5, SDO to PB4, and SDI to PB5.
The ESP8266 Click module is installed in the motherboard’s mikroBUS socket. The onboard MCU, LED, and socket connections are documented in the development-board schematic. The FPGA–MCU DIP switches are kept open to prevent interference on shared pins.


Calculations
SPI clock:
With the baud-rate field set to 3, the clock divider is
\[
D=2^{3+1}=16.
\]
Therefore,
\[
f_{\mathrm{SCLK}}=\frac{f_{\mathrm{SPI1}}}{16}.
\]
For an 80 MHz SPI1 peripheral clock,
\[
f_{\mathrm{SCLK}}=5\text{ MHz},
\qquad
T_{\mathrm{SCLK}}=200\text{ ns}.
\]
Temperature conversion:
The received bytes are combined into a signed 16-bit value:
\[
T=\frac{\operatorname{int16}(256\,\mathrm{MSB}+\mathrm{LSB})}{256}.
\]
For example, an MSB of 0x19 and LSB of 0x20 give
\[
T=\frac{25(256)+32}{256}
=25.125^\circ\text{C}.
\]
Resolution and signed range:
The 12-bit setting provides increments of
\[
\Delta T=\frac{1}{16}=0.0625^\circ\text{C}.
\]
Signed decoding supports the required endpoints:
\[
\texttt{0xF600}\rightarrow -2560/256=-10^\circ\text{C},
\]
\[
\texttt{0x1E00}\rightarrow 7680/256=30^\circ\text{C}.
\]


Oscilloscope Trace


Expand to see SPI read trace







Figure 2: Complete DS1722 LSB-register read. CH1/yellow: MISO; CH2/green: MOSI; CH4/pink: CE; CH3/blue: SCLK.






SPI Read Transaction
The oscilloscope capture shows one complete read of the DS1722 temperature low-byte register. From top to bottom, the traces are MISO (yellow, CH1), MOSI (green, CH2), CE (pink, CH4), and SCLK (blue, CH3). MOSI connects STM32 pin PB5 to the sensor’s SDI input, while MISO connects the sensor’s SDO output to STM32 pin PB4. PB0 controls CE, and PA5 supplies SCLK.
Address transfer. The transaction begins when the STM32 raises CE. The DS1722 uses an active-high chip enable, so CE remains high throughout both clock bursts. During the first eight clocks, the STM32 transmits the register address 00000001 (0x01) on MOSI, most significant bit first. This address selects the temperature low-byte register. The SPI interface uses CPOL = 0 and CPHA = 1: SCLK is low when idle, data changes on rising edges, and the receiving device samples data on falling edges. MOSI therefore rises for the final address bit, and the sensor samples that 1 on the eighth falling edge.
Pause between bytes. After the address byte, SCLK briefly stops while the STM32 finishes the first byte-transfer function and prepares the next transfer. CE stays high, so the sensor remains selected. MOSI holds the final address bit at a high level during this pause. This does not transmit additional ones because no sampling edges occur while the clock is stopped.
Data transfer. During the second eight-clock burst, the STM32 sends a dummy byte of 0x00 on MOSI. Sending this byte generates the clocks needed for the sensor to return its data on MISO. The STM32 samples MISO on each falling edge, and its SPI hardware assembles the received bits into a byte. The returned bit pattern in this capture appears to be 00100000, or 0x20.
The initial high MISO level before the response is not temperature data. During the address phase, the DS1722 output is high impedance, meaning the sensor is not actively driving the line. A high voltage during that interval cannot be interpreted as a valid transmitted bit. Only the response during the second clock burst is decoded.
Temperature interpretation. The low byte contributes the fractional portion of the temperature encoding. For the observed value:
\[
\frac{\texttt{0x20}}{256}
=
\frac{32}{256}
=
0.125^\circ\mathrm{C}.
\]
This capture alone does not establish the complete temperature. The program reads the high-byte register at address 0x02 in a separate transaction, then combines the two bytes into a signed 16-bit value:
\[
T =
\frac{\operatorname{int16}\left(256\,\mathrm{MSB}+\mathrm{LSB}\right)}
{256}.
\]
For example, a high byte of 0x16 combined with the captured low byte of 0x20 would represent 22.125°C. This is an illustrative calculation; the high byte is not shown in this capture. The driver performs separate transactions because its register-read function reads one byte at a time. Each transaction contains eight address clocks and eight data clocks, regardless of the sensor’s selected measurement resolution.
Timing comparison. Using the screenshot’s horizontal scale of 840 ns per division, the interval between consecutive rising edges within a clock burst is approximately 200 ns. One clock cycle transfers one bit, so the estimated bit period and clock frequency are:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bit}} \approx 200\ \mathrm{ns},
\qquad
f_{\mathrm{SCLK}} =
\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{bit}}}
\approx 5\ \mathrm{MHz}.
\]
The clock’s high and low intervals appear approximately equal, indicating a duty cycle near 50%. The estimated frequency is consistent with operation near the DS1722’s specified maximum of 5 MHz.
After the final data bit has been received and the SPI transfer has finished, the STM32 lowers CE to end the transaction.

title: Lab 6: SPI and the Internet of Things
text:
Conclusion
This lab demonstrated SPI communication between the STM32L432KC and DS1722 and UART communication with the ESP8266. The webpage displays temperature, controls the LED, and allows selection of 8–12-bit sensor resolution. The annotated oscilloscope capture shows a complete register-read transaction with an estimated 200 ns bit period, corresponding to approximately 5 MHz. Debugging the request handling and temperature formatting helped distinguish sensor configuration from how readings are displayed.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
The STM32L432KC plays the provided Für Elise score through an LM386 amplifier and an 8 \Omega speaker. TIM16 generates each square-wave pitch on PA6, while TIM6 measures note and rest durations.
Result: The design plays the supplied song at the specified pitches and durations, including rests. A 10 k\Omega potentiometer controls the volume.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
The STM32L432KC plays the provided Für Elise score through an LM386 amplifier and an 8 \Omega speaker. TIM16 generates each square-wave pitch on PA6, while TIM6 measures note and rest durations.
Result: The design plays the supplied song at the specified pitches and durations, including rests. A 10 k\Omega potentiometer controls the volume.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Hardware

Circuit






Figure 1: External LM386 amplifier schematic. All pin names, pin numbers, component values, polarities, and junctions are labeled.



The complete on-board design is available in the E155 Development Board schematic.
However, for this lab, the MCU was placed directly onto the breadboard not using the development board. The LM386 amplifier was connected to the MCU and a potentiometer was added to control the volume.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Software and MCU Design

Program flow

Configure flash latency for an 80 MHz system clock.
Configure the PLL for an 80 MHz clock.
configure PA6 for alternate function 14 (TIM16_CH1).
Configure TIM16 for PWM pitch generation.
Configure TIM6 as a 1 ms duration timer.
Read each {frequency, duration} pair from the supplied score.
Generate the pitch or disable the output for a rest.
Stop when a duration of zero is encountered.

The implementation uses manually defined base addresses, register structures, and bit masks. It does not use the STM32 CMSIS device header.


Clock configuration
The 4 MHz MSI clock is multiplied by the PLL:

f_{SYS}=f_{MSI}\left(\frac{N}{M}\right)\frac{1}{R}


f_{SYS}=4\text{ MHz}\left(\frac{40}{1}\right)\frac{1}{2}
=80\text{ MHz}



Timer configuration
Both timers use PSC = 79:

f_{\text{counter}}
=
\frac{f_{\text{timer input}}}{PSC+1}
=
\frac{80\text{ MHz}}{79+1}
=
1\text{ MHz}

Each timer count therefore lasts 1 \mus.
TIM6 uses ARR = 999:

T_{update}=\frac{ARR+1}{1\text{ MHz}}
=\frac{1000}{1\text{ MHz}}
=1\text{ ms}

A duration of D milliseconds is generated by waiting for D TIM6 update events.


Pitch calculations
For a desired frequency f_d:

N=\left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{f_d}\right\rfloor,
\qquad ARR=N-1,
\qquad CCR1=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{2}\right\rfloor

The resulting pitch is:

f_a=\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{ARR+1}

Example for 220 Hz:

N=\left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{220}\right\rfloor=4545


ARR=4545-1=4544


f_a=\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{4545}=220.022\text{ Hz}


\%\text{ error}=\frac{|220.022-220|}{220}\times100\%=0.010\%



Accuracy of all notes
For every nonzero score frequency at or below 1000 Hz, the period contains at least 1000 timer counts. Truncation changes the calculated period by less than one count, so the frequency error is bounded by:

\%\text{ error}<\frac{1}{1000}\times100\%=0.1\%

Therefore, all nonzero notes in the supplied Für Elise score can be reproduced within the required 1% accuracy. Testing 220 Hz and 1000 Hz alone is not a mathematical proof; the timer-resolution bound supplies the proof for the intermediate frequencies.


Supported limits
TIM16 has a 16-bit auto-reload register. With the fixed 1 MHz timer clock:

f_{min}=\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{65{,}536}=15.26\text{ Hz}

A meaningful 50% duty-cycle waveform requires at least two timer counts:

f_{max}=\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2}=500\text{ kHz}

The delay function has 1 ms resolution:

D_{min}=1\text{ ms}

For its uint32_t argument:

D_{max}=2^{32}-1\text{ ms}=49.71\text{ days}

The signed int score array limits a stored positive duration to approximately 24.86 days.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
AI Prototype and Reflection

AI Prototype Prompt

Create register-level STM32L432KC timer code that uses TIM16 to generate pitches on PA6 and TIM6 to control note durations and rests.

AI was used to prototype the timer structure and identify edge cases in pitch generation. The prototype suggested separating pitch generation and note timing between TIM16 and TIM6. It also highlighted the need to handle frequency == 0 before the division used to calculate ARR, preventing division by zero during rests. The final register addresses, bit fields, calculations, wiring, and measured behavior were checked against the STM32 and LM386 documentation and verified on the physical system.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Mission
Water quality can change substantially within the first few meters below the surface, but collecting repeatable measurements at multiple depths usually requires specialized equipment. We set out to determine whether a small, low-cost AUV could gather useful environmental data during a controlled vertical dive.
The robot needed to carry four analog sensing channels, maintain a consistent sensor orientation, protect its electronics from salt water, and return recoverable data after deployment. The sensing budget was constrained to roughly $50, which motivated the use of inexpensive solar panels as relative light sensors and concentrated most of the budget on the pH probe.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
System architecture
Pressure served as the independent depth coordinate for every other measurement. Each analog sensor passed through a channel-specific conditioning circuit before reaching the Teensy ADC. The deployment log was then converted from ADC counts to voltage and from voltage to engineering units with empirical calibration equations.





flowchart LR
  P[MPX5700 pressure] --> CP[Offset + gain]
  T[47 kΩ thermistor] --> CT[Divider + buffer + offset]
  H[Glass pH electrode] --> CH[High-impedance interface + shielding]
  L[Two solar panels] --> CL[Attenuation + offset]
  CP --> ADC[Teensy ADC]
  CT --> ADC
  CH --> ADC
  CL --> ADC
  ADC --> LOG[Deployment log]
  LOG --> MATLAB[MATLAB calibration and analysis]
  MATLAB --> DEPTH[Depth-resolved profiles]

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Sensor and circuit design
The raw sensor outputs occupied only part of the Teensy’s 0-3.3 V input range, so the analog front end used buffers, attenuation, offset, and gain stages to increase usable resolution while preventing overvoltage. A 12 V battery powered the robot, and an onboard regulator supplied a stable 5 V rail to the sensors and MCP601/MCP602 op-amps.








Channel
Sensor and purpose
Conditioning and calibration




Depth
MPX5700 pressure sensor
Offset and gain mapped the expected 0-3 m signal into the ADC range; pool calibration produced h = -1.4708V + 3.9236.


Temperature
Murata 47 kΩ NTC thermistor
A divider and unity-gain buffer prevented loading before the offset stage; processing used T = -11.854V + 32.424.


pH
Glass-electrode interface module
A high-input-impedance path, added gain, and a grounded Faraday cage reduced noise; buffer calibration produced pH = 0.912V + 6.538.


Relative light
Two ZW-5050-3V solar panels
Attenuation protected the ADC from bright conditions; a quadratic calibration converted voltage to estimated lumens.









Figure 1: Calibration curves for pressure, temperature, relative light, and pH. The empirical fits were used to process the field data.









Figure 2: pH and solar-panel interface designs. Both channels use offset and gain stages to map their expected outputs into the ADC range.



The pH circuit required extra care because the glass electrode and its interface were sensitive to high source impedance, long leads, motor PWM, and nearby wiring. We placed that channel on a separate breadboard inside a grounded copper-and-aluminum Faraday cage. The shielding reduced electrical noise, but it could not correct the chemistry mismatch between freshwater buffer calibration and seawater deployment.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Mechanical integration






Figure 3: Mechanical drawing, aerial view, and side view of the completed robot with sensor locations labeled.



The PVC frame was designed primarily for vertical movement. The pressure sensor, thermistor, and pH probe faced downward so their sensing surfaces sampled approximately the same depth. The solar panels faced upward to receive incident light, and the electronics enclosure sat near the center of the frame. Buoyant components were placed above heavier components to provide passive restoring stability.
The estimated robot mass was 3.3701 kg, while the calculated buoyant force was 39.43 N. The center of buoyancy was estimated at 0.135 m above the bottom of the frame, slightly above the 0.116 m center of mass. That separation helped the vehicle return toward an upright orientation after small disturbances.
The original design used four vertical motors. Two motors drew excessive current and produced motherboard reliability problems, so the final configuration used two diagonal vertical thrusters. This reduced electrical load while preserving a balanced vertical force arrangement.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Testing and field deployment
The robot progressed through pool calibration, freshwater integration testing, and final saltwater deployment. Roberts Pool provided a controlled 0-3 m reference for the pressure channel. A later test at pHake Lake exposed a major waterproofing failure: water entered the electronics enclosure, activated motor-controller warnings, and caused several sensor channels to rail or short.
That failure changed the Dana Point procedure. Cable penetrations were resealed with marine epoxy, the empty enclosure was leak-checked before reinstalling electronics, and the team adopted a staged-depth plan. A 10 m tether provided immediate recovery, and 0.5 m tape marks supplied a visual depth reference. Before each launch, the serial monitor was used to confirm plausible outputs from all four sensor channels.




Top view of the completed AUV showing the central electronics enclosure and sensor placement.





Tethered recovery of the AUV during field testing.



The final dataset was recorded on April 25, 2026. Early complications reduced the planned 9 m profile to a safer 3 m target, allowing the team to collect a complete descend-hold-return dataset without risking the vehicle.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Results






Figure 4: Dana Point time series. Pressure defines the dive profile; temperature and both light channels change during descent, while the pH channel clips.









Figure 5: Measurements plotted against pressure-derived depth with uncertainty and model comparisons.





Pressure
The pressure channel was the strongest quantitative result. It captured the complete descend-hold-return motion and measured a maximum depth of 2.61 ± 0.05 m. Its pool-calibration RMS residual was only 0.0462 m.


Temperature
The thermistor decreased from 23.1 ± 0.3 °C before immersion to 18.0 ± 0.6 °C at the deepest interval. A field thermometer measured 18.7 °C at the surface, so the channel demonstrated a useful relative trend but retained an absolute offset.


Relative light
The two solar-panel channels fell by approximately 30 ± 3% and 38 ± 6%. Exponential fits yielded attenuation coefficients of 0.16 ± 0.08 m⁻¹ and 0.24 ± 0.11 m⁻¹, although tilt, waves, shadowing, and broadband response limit quantitative interpretation.


pH
The pH output converged near 6.54, while field ground truth was approximately 7.4. The nearly constant, clipped response was excluded as environmental data and treated as evidence that the probe required seawater-specific calibration and longer settling time.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
What the failures taught us
The project produced useful data because failures were treated as design information rather than hidden from the final analysis.

Waterproofing must be verified before electronics are installed. The pHake Lake flood led to separate enclosure testing, cleaner penetrator holes, marine epoxy sealing, and immediate tethered recovery.
Calibration must match the deployment environment. Low-salinity pH buffers did not reproduce the liquid-junction behavior of the glass electrode in seawater.
Relative and absolute accuracy are different. The thermistor clearly followed a cooling trend, but its offset against the field thermometer prevented a strong absolute-temperature claim.
The sensor can disturb the measurement. Solar-panel orientation, robot tilt, surface ripples, and frame shadows all affected the apparent light profile.
One successful dive is not enough for repeatability. Future deployments should use repeated descents with 20-30 second holds at fixed depths to separate real water-column structure from sensor lag and vehicle motion.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Team and next iteration
This was a team project with Luke Pratt, Megan Tran, and Lucy Will. The next version should use seawater-matched pH standards, sealed modular gain settings, improved high-impedance shielding, and repeated fixed-depth profiles. The tether, staged-depth testing, and serial-monitor preflight checks should remain because they made field failures recoverable.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and testing methodology
The column synchronizer brings the asynchronous, active-low keypad columns into the FPGA clock domain. The keypad scanner drives the rows and produces a 16-bit key map for each scan. The debouncer accepts a key map after it remains consistent; the decoder determines whether zero, one, or multiple keys are active and produces a hexadecimal key code. The controller decides when to shift a new key into the two display registers. The existing multiplexing circuit selects which register drives the shared seven-segment decoder.
I tested the new modules individually before simulating the complete system. The testbenches exercised reset, key changes, held keys, multiple keys, and the resulting display updates.

Block diagram






Figure 1: Top-level block diagram of the Lab 3 FPGA design.









Figure 2: Detailed drawings of the column synchronizer, keypad scanner, debouncer, decoder, and controller.





Controller FSM






Figure 3: State transition diagram for the keypad controller.



The controller starts in Ready. A stable single-key sample is accepted once and moves the controller to Hold. Repeated samples of the same held key do not change the display. If additional keys are pressed, the controller moves to Multiple and holds the displayed digits. When the multiple-key input becomes one stable key, it accepts that remaining key and returns to Hold.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
AI Prototype Summary
AI assistance was used to answer this prompt:

Write SystemVerilog logic that determines whether a 16-bit keypad map contains any key or exactly one key.



AI-assisted key detection code

assign any_key = |keys;
assign one_key = any_key &&
                 ((keys & (keys - 16'b1)) == 16'b0);

Reflection: AI showed me a shorter way to detect whether exactly one keypad key is active. My current key_decoder uses a case statement that sets one_key for each valid one-key pattern. The generated expression instead uses the fact that a value with exactly one set bit becomes zero when ANDed with one less than itself.
My code already uses |keys for any_key, so that part was not an improvement. The 16-entry case is still needed to map each key position to its hexadecimal key_code. The new expression could replace only the one_key checks. I checked that both methods agree for all 65,536 two-state key maps, but I have not compared their synthesized resource usage.

title: Lab 5: Motor Velocity with Encoder Interrupts
text:
Program Flow



Main loop and encoder interrupt handlers.


TIM2 counts microseconds. Both rising and falling edges of encoder channels A and B trigger interrupts.

title: Lab 5: Motor Velocity with Encoder Interrupts
text:
Calculations
Both edges of both encoder channels are counted:
\[
N = 408 \times 4 = 1632\text{ counts/rev}.
\]
Angular resolution:
\[
\Delta\theta = \frac{360^\circ}{1632}
= 0.221^\circ/\text{count}.
\]
Update rate:
\[
f_{\text{report}} = \frac{1}{0.250}
= 4\text{ Hz}.
\]
Velocity: For count change \(\Delta C\) over elapsed time \(\Delta t\) in seconds,
\[
v = \frac{\Delta C}{1632\Delta t}.
\]
Approximately 46,000 counts over 10 seconds gives
\[
v = \frac{46{,}000}{1632(10)}
\approx 2.82\text{ rev/s}.
\]
Velocity resolution: One count in a 250 ms window corresponds to
\[
\Delta v = \frac{1}{1632(0.250)}
\approx 0.00245\text{ rev/s}.
\]
Low-speed estimate: Using the interval between consecutive same-direction edges,
\[
|v| = \frac{10^6}{1632T_{\text{edge}}}\text{ rev/s},
\]
where \(T_{\text{edge}}\) is in microseconds.
Direction: The order of changes in channels A and B determines whether the encoder count increases or decreases.

title: Lab 5: Motor Velocity with Encoder Interrupts
text:
Interrupts Compared with Polling
Approximately 46,000 encoder transitions were counted in 10 seconds:
\[
f_{\text{edge}} = \frac{46{,}000}{10}
= 4600\text{ transitions/s}.
\]
The average time between transitions was
\[
T_{\text{edge}} = \frac{10^6}{4600}
\approx217\ \mu\text{s}.
\]
A polling interval of 100 μs would require 10,000 pin checks per second, compared with approximately 4,600 encoder interrupts per second at this speed. Polling repeatedly checks the inputs even when nothing changes; interrupts require processing only when an edge occurs.
Polling must remain faster than the shortest edge interval, including time spent calculating and printing. Interrupts allow encoder counting to continue during those main-loop operations, provided interrupt latency and processing time are short enough.
This is a calculated comparison; a separate polling implementation was not tested. The 217 μs value is an average and does not guarantee that a particular polling interval captures every edge.

title: Multicycle RISC-V Processor
text:
What I built
The design is organized as a hierarchy of small reusable modules. A controller decodes the current instruction and advances a finite-state machine. The datapath holds the program counter, instruction, register operands, memory data, and ALU result between cycles. A unified memory stores both instructions and data, so an address multiplexer selects either the program counter during instruction fetch or the computed data address during a load or store.





flowchart LR
  MEM[Unified memory]
  CTRL[Controller]

  subgraph PATH[Datapath]
    PC[Program counter]
    IR[Instruction register]
    RF[32 × 32 register file]
    EXT[Immediate extension]
    ALU[ALU]
    AOUT[ALUOut register]
    MDR[Memory-data register]
  end

  PC -->|instruction address| MEM
  MEM -->|instruction| IR
  MEM -->|load data| MDR
  IR --> RF
  IR --> EXT
  RF -->|operands| ALU
  EXT -->|immediate| ALU
  PC --> ALU
  ALU --> AOUT
  AOUT -->|data address| MEM
  RF -->|store data| MEM
  IR -->|opcode and function fields| CTRL
  ALU -->|zero| CTRL
  CTRL -. control signals .-> PC
  CTRL -. control signals .-> RF
  CTRL -. control signals .-> ALU






The structural modules include parameterized registers, two- and three-input multiplexers, an ALU, a 32-register file, immediate extension logic, instruction and ALU decoders, the main finite-state machine, and the top-level processor and memory wrappers.

title: Multicycle RISC-V Processor
text:
Multicycle control
Each instruction begins in the same fetch and decode states. Later states depend on the opcode. Intermediate values are stored in registers so the ALU can be reused for incrementing the program counter, forming an address, performing an arithmetic operation, and evaluating a branch.








State or path
Main operation
Important control action




Fetch
Read the instruction and calculate PC + 4
Write the instruction register and program counter


Decode
Read source registers and form the immediate
Select the next execution path from the opcode


Load/store address
Calculate rs1 + immediate
Save the effective address in ALUOut


Load
Read unified memory, then write rd
Select memory data for register writeback


Store
Write rs2 to unified memory
Assert MemWrite for one cycle


R-type / I-type ALU
Perform the decoded ALU operation
Write the saved ALU result to rd


Branch
Compare register operands
Update the PC only when the branch condition is true


JAL
Save the return address and redirect the PC
Write PC + 4 to rd and load the jump target


AUIPC
Add the upper immediate to the instruction PC
Write the sum directly to rd




Extending the processor for AUIPC
The original immediate path handled I-, S-, B-, and J-type encodings. I added an ImmIsU control signal so the extender can recognize the U-type format and concatenate Instr[31:12] with twelve zeros. The opcode decoder routes AUIPC to a new controller state, where the ALU adds that immediate to the saved instruction address and writes the result back to the destination register.
This change touched the instruction decoder, immediate extender, controller interface, datapath, and main state machine. Keeping it as a separate control path made the extension explicit without changing the behavior of the existing instruction formats.

title: Multicycle RISC-V Processor
text:
Supported instruction behavior
The submitted design exercises the following processor paths:

Arithmetic and logic: add, sub, and, or, and slt
Immediate arithmetic through I-type ALU instructions
Memory access: lw and sw
Control flow: conditional branch and jal
PC-relative address generation: auipc

The ALU produces addition, subtraction, bitwise AND, bitwise OR, and signed less-than results. Its zero output feeds the branch decision logic. Register x0 remains hardwired to zero because reads return zero and writes to address zero are suppressed.

title: Multicycle RISC-V Processor
text:
Verification strategy
I loaded the test program from memfile.dat and observed the top-level processor interface throughout the run. The waveform tracks the clock, reset, memory write data, data address, and MemWrite. This gives a compact end-to-end check: a correct final store depends on all preceding instructions producing the right register values and control-flow decisions.






Figure 1: Full simulation waveform for the machine-code test program. The short MemWrite pulse near the end marks the final store.



The full waveform shows the address and write-data buses changing as the processor fetches instructions and executes memory operations. MemWrite remains low during instruction fetches and calculations, then pulses only during the store state.

Final memory write






Figure 2: Detailed view of the final store. WriteData holds 0x00001067; the following store cycle presents address 0x00000054 and asserts MemWrite.



The zoomed view captures the result of the complete test. WriteData has settled to 0x00001067 before the store, and the data address advances to 0x00000054, which is byte address 84. The controller then asserts MemWrite, committing the value to unified memory. Because this is the expected terminal write, it demonstrates that the processor reached the correct point in the program with the correct computed result.

title: Multicycle RISC-V Processor
text:
What I learned
This project made the boundary between datapath and control much more concrete. A multicycle processor is less about writing one large block of logic and more about coordinating when each value becomes valid, where it is stored, and which shared resource uses it next. Most debugging came down to following those values one cycle at a time through the finite-state machine.
Adding AUIPC also showed how an ISA feature propagates through the entire design. Even a seemingly small instruction requires agreement among encoding, immediate generation, ALU inputs, controller sequencing, and register writeback. The final program-level waveform was therefore more valuable than checking the new state in isolation.
